title: Persistent Hotspots and Seasonal Habitat Use of Indo‐Pacific Bottlenose Dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) in an Urban Marine Protected Area
content:
ABSTRACT

Understanding wildlife distribution is essential for identifying critical habitats, monitoring responses to environmental change and informing conservation strategies. We used long-term sighting data (1993–2020) and generalised additive modelling (GAM) to quantify and characterise the long-term spatiotemporal distribution of Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) in South Australia's urbanised Adelaide Dolphin Sanctuary (ADS). The top-performing GAM indicated that dolphin presence was influenced by spatial (latitude and longitude) and temporal (year) variables, with seasonal variation in these relationships. Dolphin presence increased from 1993 to the early 2000s, with high probabilities of occurrence maintained over the last decade. Although some inter-annual variability was evident, no clear long-term decline was observed. Four major hotspots of dolphin use were identified in the ADS: Angas Inlet, North Arm, Light Passage and Outer Harbour. In winter, predicted presence was highest at Light Passage and Angas Inlet, whereas in spring, it was concentrated in the southern ADS, particularly around Angas Inlet and North Arm. Depth (m) as a predictor variable was not statistically significant; thus, these distribution patterns likely reflect fine-scale habitat preferences and resource availability. The consistent use of specific areas indicates persistent habitat preferences and suggests that these locations as ecologically important. However, the ecological drivers of these preferences remain unclear. Future research should focus on fine-scale, site-specific data collection, including benthic habitat mapping, water quality monitoring, prey availability and spatial risk assessments, to improve understanding of ecosystem functioning in dolphin hotspots.
